# Generate Fixtures Rather Than Commit Them

**Decision.** Ship a four-line generator for the 1 MB / 5 MB / 10 MB inputs used to time RSA, and
`.gitignore` the outputs — rather than committing 16 MB of filler.

**Date.** 2026-07-25 (the publishing commit), `labs/04_asymmetric_ciphers/` of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]].

## Why

The argument is written in the script's own docstring and turns on a property of the measurement
rather than on repository hygiene generally:

> "each file is a single character repeated to the required length ... they are generated rather than
> committed: 16 MB of a repeated character is the largest thing that could go in this repository and
> the least informative."
> — Cybersecurity-Engineering-Laboratories/labs/04_asymmetric_ciphers/generate_test_files.py, 2026-07-25

**Largest and least informative** is the whole case. Lab 04 measures how RSA encryption cost scales
with input size, so the *content* of the input is irrelevant by construction — see
[[symmetric-vs-asymmetric-cryptography]]. A fixture whose content does not matter is a fixture that
should be described rather than stored, and four lines of Python describe it exactly.

The README states the rule in the same section as the two key-material rules, which is where it
belongs — all three are about what does not go in a repository:

> "Fixtures are generated, not stored. Lab 4 times RSA against 1 MB, 5 MB and 10 MB inputs whose
> content is irrelevant to the measurement."
> — Cybersecurity-Engineering-Laboratories/README.md, 2026-07-25

## Alternatives rejected

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| **Commit the three files** | 16 MB of a repeated character; every clone pays for it forever, and git stores it in history even if later deleted |
| **Git LFS** | infrastructure and a dependency for data that can be recreated in a second — and this repo has no `.gitattributes` at all |
| **Commit smaller files and scale the results** | changes the measurement; the whole experiment is about size |
| **Document the sizes in prose and generate by hand** | the reader would have to reconstruct the fixtures from a description, which is what the script already is — only unreliable |

**TODO:** only the first is evidenced as considered ("the largest thing that could go in this
repository"). The rest are stated here as the alternatives, not as recorded deliberation.

## What the script gets right beyond the decision

It is 50 lines of stdlib-only Python and worth reading as a small example of the repo's habits:

- **Writes in 1 MB chunks**, so producing the 10 MB file does not need 10 MB of memory — the docstring
  says so at the function that does it.
- **`pathlib` throughout**, with the destination as an optional argument defaulting to the script's
  own directory.
- **Returns an exit code from `main`** and prints the byte count of each file written, so a run is
  self-verifying.
- **`.gitignore` carries `*mb.txt`** with a comment naming the script that produces them — the
  ignore rule and the generator point at each other, so neither can be found without the other.

That last detail is what makes this durable rather than merely tidy. An ignore rule with no stated
producer becomes a mystery within a year; here the tree explains itself. Compare
[[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]].

## The general form

**If an artefact is deterministic and cheap to reproduce, commit the producer, not the product.** The
same reasoning appears elsewhere in this source set from the opposite direction — see
[[generated-audit-artifact]], where the output *is* committed precisely because it is the evidence
rather than an input. The test is what the artefact is for: an input that only needs to exist should
be generated; an output that needs to be reviewable should be committed.

The sibling decision in the same README section is [[omit-rsa-private-key-screenshot]] — the other
half of "what does not belong in this repository".
